Empirical Research Plan: Do Institutions Cause Cross-Country Income Differences?

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Cross–sectional two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) design.

Why IV?  
•  We need exogenous variation in today’s institutional quality that is plausibly unrelated to contemporaneous productivity shocks.  
•  Historical European settler mortality provides a source of quasi-random variation: it determined whether Europeans could settle permanently and, consequently, the kind of colonial institutions they transplanted (inclusive vs. extractive).  
•  The mortality environment in the 17th–19th centuries is predetermined with respect to today’s incomes and is no longer a first-order constraint on production (malaria can be cured, yellow-fever vaccines exist). Hence it can serve as an external instrument for modern institutions.

Alternative strategies (DID, RDD, event study) are not feasible because (i) the institutional “treatment” is not sharply timed, (ii) countries do not share a common pre-trend, and (iii) no obvious running variable around a cutoff exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):  
•  INST_i  ≡ average 1985-1995 protection-against-expropriation index (0–10, higher = safer property rights).

Instrument:  
•  SETTLER_MORT_i  ≡ natural log of annualized mortality of European soldiers, sailors, and bishops stationed 1600–1870 (deaths per 1,000 mean strength).

“Treatment” interpretation: A country is effectively “treated” with good institutions if settler mortality was low enough for Europeans to settle and transplant inclusive institutions. Countries with very high mortality form the implicit control group.

No timing dimension—this is a one-shot historical instrument.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Historical settler mortality strongly predicts today’s institutional quality.  
 Plausibility: Colonies where Europeans could survive did receive large‐scale settlement, documented by migration data and qualitative history.

A2. Exclusion (exogeneity): Conditional on controls, settler mortality affects current income only through institutions, not via other channels (e.g., persistent disease burden, geography).  
 Plausibility: Tropical diseases that killed Europeans affected them far more than indigenous populations and are now largely treatable. We will control for present-day malaria prevalence, latitude, climate, and natural-resource endowments.

A3. Independence (as-good-as-random conditional on controls): Mortality rates were driven by ecology, not by unobserved pre-colonial development prospects.  
 Plausibility: The sample is limited to areas without prior European settlements, reducing reverse causality.

A4. Monotonicity: Lower mortality never reduced the probability of receiving good institutions (no “defiers”).  
 Plausibility: Historical narratives suggest a monotonic relationship—where Europeans could survive they preferred settler colonies with English common law and elected assemblies.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One colony’s settler mortality does not directly affect another colony’s contemporaneous GDP once we condition on institutions.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable at the country level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Direct disease channel—areas that were deadly for Europeans were (and may still be) unhealthy for _everyone_, lowering current productivity.  
• Mitigation: Include current life expectancy, malaria ecology index, and tropical-disease prevalence as controls; test whether mortality predicts income after controlling for institutions (reduced-form vs. second stage).

Threat 2: Omitted geographic/cultural factors correlated with mortality (soil, climate, colonial origin).  
• Mitigation: Extensive baseline controls (latitude, rainfall, temperature, humidity, soil quality, natural resources, ethnolinguistic fragmentation) and dummies for continental region, legal origin, and former colonizer.

Threat 3: Measurement error in mortality data (small samples of soldiers, patchy coverage).  
• Mitigation: Use log transformation; drop observations with imputed rather than archival mortality figures; run robustness with alternative mortality compilations; report first-stage F-statistic to show relevance is not driven by noise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Libraries
# --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # for IV estimation
library(lmtest)         # for coeftest & Wald tests
library(sandwich)       # robust vcov
library(tidyverse)      # misc utilities

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load and Merge Data
# --------------------------------------------------------------
wdi   <- fread("GDP_WDI_1995.csv")           # assume country, gdp_pc_1995
hj88  <- fread("HallJones_output_1988.csv")  # country, output_worker_1988
inst  <- fread("PRS_expro_85_95.csv")        # country, expro_index
pol   <- fread("Polity_variables.csv")       # country, exec_constraints_1900
mort  <- fread("Settler_mortality.csv")      # country, mort_per_1000
geo   <- fread("Geography_controls.csv")     # latitude, temp, humidity, etc.

# Merge on ISO code or country name
dt <- reduce(list(wdi, hj88, inst, pol, mort, geo), ~merge(.x, .y, by="country", all=FALSE))

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Variable Construction
# --------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- dt[ , `:=` (
  ln_gdppc95      = log(gdp_pc_1995),
  ln_output88     = log(output_worker_1988),
  institutions    = expro_index,                    # 0–10 scale
  ln_settler_mort = log(mort_per_1000),
  abs_latitude    = abs(latitude)
)]

# optional: scale institutions to SD = 1 for elasticities
dt[, inst_z := scale(institutions)]

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Baseline 2SLS: ln GDPpc 1995 on Institutions (IV = ln settler mortality)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- ln_gdppc95 ~ institutions + abs_latitude + temp + humidity +
                               soil_quality + natural_resources +
                               malaria_prev + factor(continent) | 
                             abs_latitude + temp + humidity +
                               soil_quality + natural_resources +
                               malaria_prev + factor(continent) + ln_settler_mort

model_2sls <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt, vcov = cluster ~ continent)
summary(model_2sls, stage = 1)       # shows first stage F-stat

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Robustness Check: Alternative outcome (Hall & Jones 1988)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula2 <- ln_output88 ~ institutions + controls |
                              controls + ln_settler_mort

model_alt <- feols(iv_formula2, data = dt, vcov = cluster ~ continent)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Weak-instrument & Over-ID tests (if we add another IV)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# First-stage F-stat is printed above; overid if extra IVs available
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Sign (+): Stronger property-rights institutions should raise income.

Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope):  
Historical estimates suggest that a one-standard-deviation (≈ 2.5 points on the 0–10 index) increase in institutional quality raises log GDP per capita by roughly 0.6–1.0, i.e., 80–170 percent higher income. I would expect a midpoint of about 0.8 log points (≈ 120 percent).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F > 10) …………………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable ………………………… 0.5  
C3: No omitted channels after controls …………………… 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ………………………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA / no interference …………………………………… 1  

Overall score: 4 / 5 (reasonable but not bullet-proof).
